sections:
**“How big a model can my hardware run” is a problem you can do by hand.**
This guide gives the hardware-side key facts (only figures stated on official spec pages),
then the composition method for the cost math.

By discipline this site stores no card prices or rental rates and gives no purchase advice.
Figures change when vendors revise; the re-check date is in the footer.

Two numbers decide “can it run”: memory capacity decides how big a model fits,
and memory bandwidth decides how many tokens per second the decode phase can emit.

- NVIDIA H100 SXM: 80GB memory, 3.35TB/s bandwidth (official spec page).
- NVIDIA H100 NVL: 94GB memory, 3.9TB/s bandwidth (both columns on the same page).
- NVIDIA A100 80GB: HBM2e, 1,935 GB/s (PCIe) / 2,039 GB/s (SXM) bandwidth.
- NVIDIA RTX 4090: 24GB GDDR6X (consumer card; the official page states no bandwidth figure).
- Apple MacBook Pro (M5 family): unified memory starting at 16/24/32GB,
  up to 128GB on higher configs — CPU and GPU share the same memory (official spec page).

Honest note: AMD's consumer-card spec pages could not be verified this pass (site unreachable),
so this site records no AMD figures — unknown stays unknown, no copying from second-hand spec sheets.
Power draw, interconnect, FP8 support and other details follow the official pages and are not expanded here.

Every token the generation phase produces requires reading the model weights in full once more.
The per-second token ceiling of single-request decode ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token.

An 8B model's FP16 weights are about 16GB. On 3.35TB/s bandwidth the
theoretical ceiling is roughly 200 tokens/second — that is the ceiling; real numbers also subtract KV-cache reads and overhead.
Quantised to 4-bit the weights are about 4GB, so the same card's ceiling is about four times higher. That is the quantisation throughput ledger.

Prefill (reading a long prompt) is the opposite: one forward pass processes many tokens, compute-bound.
So “time to first token” and “time per token” are set by two different hardware properties,
and the tuning directions are completely different.

The cost chain for online inference decomposes as:

1. Cost per token = hardware cost per hour ÷ tokens that hardware produces per hour.
2. Hourly output is set by the bandwidth math above plus concurrent batching — the bigger the batch, the more the weight read is amortised.
3. Hardware price per hour moves with the market monthly; this site does not store it, by discipline.

What you can compute yourself is the middle term. Given model size and quantisation tier, plus a concurrency number,
estimate throughput with the bandwidth math, then divide throughput into the unit price. Vendor quote pages and cloud price pages are public entry points;
this site teaches how to build the chain, it does not copy today's numbers for you.

Judgement basis for selection (not a recommendation): with high concurrency and long context, the bottleneck is KV-cache memory — watch bandwidth and capacity.
For single-machine personal use it is the opposite: the bottleneck is “does it fit” — mainly capacity and quantisation tier.

The “VRAM reverse lookup” table on this site's series pages answers “which tier your VRAM can download” from measured file sizes —
that is the user's entry point; this guide gives hardware-side facts and the conversion method, the practitioner's yardstick.
Both include weight storage and KV cache in the memory budget.

The Learn site's [VRAM](https://learn.specul.com/term/%E6%98%BE%E5%AD%98/) and
[quantisation](https://learn.specul.com/term/%E9%87%8F%E5%8C%96/) pages are user-perspective explainers;
this guide gives the hardware fact table and the composition method for the cost math.

Same concept, different depth on each side, cross-linked without duplication.
For the KV cache and batching mechanics see the previous guide, “Serving deep dive”.

This hypothetical capacity exercise is not a named model or a measured site result. A GiB is 2^30 bytes; decimal GB and GiB are not numerically interchangeable.

Assume a 10 GiB available budget and 6 GiB of weights. With assumed cache use of 2 GiB and runtime use of 1 GiB, the estimate is 9 GiB, leaving 1 GiB headroom. Cache/runtime figures are exercise assumptions; actual use depends on model, precision, context and concurrency.

Check file size, runtime support and available memory. Start with short input, record use, then increase context. If cache exceeds budget, assess shorter input, different concurrency or other tiers. Check runtime documentation for offload support.

Capacity does not predict speed or establish quality. Compare equal tasks for latency, errors and usage. This example makes no performance guarantee or purchase recommendation.

Continue to the [local-model workflow](https://tools.specul.com/mcp/guides/playbook-local-model.html), or revisit [quantization](https://learn.specul.com/term/%E9%87%8F%E5%8C%96/) to separate bit width from quality.
